title: Communication Vocabulary
keyIdea: There are three ways to speak up. Passive means you go quiet or give in, so no one hears what you need. Aggressive means you shout, blame or threaten, so the other person feels attacked. Assertive means you say what you need, calmly and with respect. An I-statement helps: "I feel upset when you talk over me. Could we take turns?" A conflict is a disagreement. You negotiate by talking it through, a helper can mediate, and a compromise is when both give up a little. The fix you agree on is the resolution.

kid: When someone upsets you, there are three ways to answer. Passive means you go quiet or give in. Aggressive means you shout, blame or threaten. Assertive is in the middle: you say what you need, calmly, and you are kind about it.

Assertive is not the same as loud. Shouting "Give it back, thief!" makes the other person feel attacked, so they fight back. Saying "That's my pencil. Please give it back" is calm and clear, and it works better. Being quiet and nice is not assertive either, if you never say what you need.

An I-statement is a good way to be assertive. Say how you feel, what they did, and what you need: "I feel sad when my book gets lost. Could we look for it together?" Start with I, not you, and talk about what happened, not about what the person is like.

A conflict is a disagreement. You negotiate when you talk it through to find a deal. A helper in the middle can mediate. A compromise is when both of you give up a little, so you both get some of what you want. The fix you agree on is the resolution. A boundary is a line you set, like "Please ask before you take my things."
adult: This topic is for ages 7 to 11. It gives children the words for healthy talk when things go wrong: passive, assertive and aggressive styles, I-statements, conflict, negotiate, mediate, compromise, resolution and boundary. With the words, a child can name what happened and choose a better way next time.

The three styles are best taught as one line, from quiet to loud, with assertive in the middle. Passive means the need is never said, so the problem stays. Aggressive means the need is said as an attack, so the other person defends. Assertive means the need is said clearly and with respect for both people. An I-statement ("I feel ... when ... Could we ...?") is the usual tool taught in schools.

Common mistakes: thinking assertive means loud or getting your own way; thinking being quiet and nice is the same as being assertive; "I feel like you are rude", which is a blame with I in front; using always and never, which start an argument; and thinking a compromise means one person gives in. Children also mix up negotiate (the two sides talk) and mediate (a third person helps).

In the lab your child slides Kai's reply from passive to aggressive and watches Jo react, sorts six replies into the three styles, builds two I-statements from pieces, shares a 20-minute break between tag and football until both get a fair part, and matches five conflict words to scenes.

familyTip: When a squabble comes up, pause and ask: "Was that passive, assertive or aggressive?" Then help your child try it again as an I-statement: "I feel ... when ... Could we ...?" Praise the calm, clear version, even if it does not get them their way.

practice.prompt: Jo takes Kai's pencil. Kai says, "That's my pencil. Please give it back." Which style is this?
practice.hint: Is Kai calm? Does he say what he needs?
practice.explain: Kai is calm and clear, and he says what he needs. That is assertive.

practice.prompt: Ruby waits {n} minutes for the swing. Then Max pushes in. Ruby says nothing and walks away. Which style is this?
practice.hint: Did Ruby say what she needed?
practice.explain: Ruby went quiet and gave in, so her need was never said. That is passive.

choices: I feel upset when you talk over me.
practice.hint: An I-statement starts with I and names a feeling.
practice.explain: "I feel upset when you talk over me" says the feeling and the action, with no blame. The others start with you and blame.

practice.prompt: Ava and Ben both want all {n} minutes of break: Ava for tag, Ben for football. Which plan is a compromise?
choices: Half the break for each game
Ben gives in and plays tag
practice.hint: In a compromise, does one person give in, or do both give a little?
practice.explain: Sharing the time means both give up a little and both get some. If one gives in, that is not a compromise.

practice.prompt: Two friends argue. A teacher stands between them and helps each one listen. What is the teacher doing?
practice.hint: Is the teacher one of the two sides, or a helper in the middle?
practice.explain: A helper in the middle who helps both sides listen is mediating. Negotiating is when the two sides talk it out.

pool.prompt: Leo says, "It doesn't matter, I don't mind," but he does mind. Which style is this?
pool.hint: Is Leo saying what he really needs?
pool.explain: Leo hides what he needs, so it is passive. Being quiet and nice is not the same as being assertive.

pool.prompt: Someone takes Zoe's seat. She shouts, "Move, or you'll be sorry!" Which style is this?
pool.hint: A threat: is it calm, or does it attack?
pool.explain: A threat attacks the other person, so it is aggressive, even if Zoe was right to want her seat back.

pool.prompt: Sam has asked {n} times to have a turn. Which reply is assertive?
choices: "I've asked a few times. Please can I have a turn now?"
"Fine, I don't want a turn anyway."
"You're so selfish. Give it to me!"
pool.hint: Look for the reply that is calm, clear and kind.
pool.explain: The first reply says what Sam needs, calmly. The second gives in (passive) and the third blames and grabs (aggressive).

pool.prompt: Mia says, "I feel like you are mean." Why is this not a good I-statement?
choices: It is really a blame about the person
It does not start with I
pool.hint: Mean is a word about the person. Is it a feeling?
pool.explain: Mean is not a feeling, it is a label for the other person. A good I-statement names a feeling, like sad, and the action: "I feel sad when you laugh at me."

pool.prompt: Two friends talk it through and agree to take turns on the bike, {n} minutes each. What is the agreement called?
pool.hint: Is this the problem, or the fix?
pool.explain: The fix that ends a conflict is the resolution. The conflict was the disagreement about the bike.

pool.prompt: Raj says, "Please ask before you borrow my things." What is Raj setting?
pool.hint: Raj is drawing a line for how others treat his things.
pool.explain: A boundary is a line you set for how others treat you or your things. Saying it calmly is assertive.

choices: Saying what you need, calmly and with respect
Getting your own way every time
Keeping quiet to stay out of trouble
pool.hint: Think of the middle of the line from quiet to loud.
pool.explain: Assertive means you say what you need, calmly, and you respect the other person too. It does not mean you always win.

pool.prompt: Which word means two sides talking it through to find a deal?
pool.hint: Is there a helper in the middle, or just the two sides?
pool.explain: To negotiate is for the two sides to talk it through. To mediate is for a third person to help them.

pool.prompt: Eli wants the blue team. Kim wants the red team. Which is a compromise?
choices: Eli plays blue today and red next time
Kim gives in, and Eli gets his way
They both stop playing for good
pool.hint: Do both of them get some of what they want?
pool.explain: Taking turns means each gives up a little and both get some. One person giving in is not a compromise.

visual.caption: I-statement or you-blame? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: I feel sad when my game gets knocked over.
I feel left out when I'm not picked.
I feel cross when you take my pens.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide a reply from passive to aggressive, sort replies, build I-statements, find a compromise, match conflict words.
